overview.summary: UI/UX designers shape how digital products such as apps and websites look and feel, and how easy they are to use.
overview.problems: They find out what users struggle with and design screens and flows that help people get things done without confusion.
overview.worksWith: Product managers, developers, researchers, other designers and users.
overview.workplaces: Technology companies, agencies, banks, start-ups, in-house teams, and freelance or remote work.

timeline.title: Team check-in
timeline.description: The designer shares progress and hears feedback from developers and any open design questions.
timeline.why: Design decisions affect many people, so the team lines up early.

timeline.title: Understanding users
timeline.description: The designer reviews research notes, user interviews, usage numbers or support complaints to see where people get stuck.
timeline.why: Designing without understanding users means guessing.

timeline.title: Sketching and designing screens
timeline.description: The designer sketches flows, then creates wireframes and layouts in design software, thinking about what appears on each screen and in what order.
timeline.why: A good structure makes a product easy to use before any visual polish is added.

timeline.title: Prototype and testing
timeline.description: The designer builds a clickable prototype and watches a few people try a task, noting where they hesitate.
timeline.why: Testing with real people shows problems that designers miss.

timeline.title: Working with developers
timeline.description: The designer explains designs, answers questions and adjusts them when something is hard to build.
timeline.why: A design only helps people if it can be built well.

timeline.title: Feedback and revisions
timeline.description: Managers and other stakeholders ask for changes, and the designer explains the reasons behind choices.
timeline.why: Designs usually change several times before they are released.

responsibilities: Mapping how users move through a product
Working with developers while the product is built
challenges: Opinions about design differ and can be subjective.
Business deadlines can leave little time for research and testing.
Users do not always behave the way designers expect.
Products have to work for people with different abilities, which takes extra care.
Competition for roles is strong, so a portfolio matters.
workEnvironment: Mostly desk and computer based, in offices or remotely, in close contact with product and engineering teams. The work mixes quiet design time with meetings, research sessions and workshops.
rewards: Making products easier for people to use
A mix of creative and analytical thinking
Seeing real people use your design
A wide range of industries to work in
tradeoffs: Subjective feedback and many people with opinions
Job titles, demand and pay that vary by employer and country
The need to keep a portfolio up to date

activity.title: Test the usability of an everyday app or website
steps: Choose a simple task, such as finding a school timetable on a website or setting an alarm on a phone.
Ask two or three people who agree to help to try it while you watch quietly.
Note where they hesitate, tap the wrong thing or look confused.
Sketch one change that would fix the biggest problem.
Note whether watching people and improving a design felt interesting.
activity.outcome: You practise watching real behaviour and turning it into design improvements.
activity.safety: Ask only people who agree to take part, never ask them to share passwords or personal information, and do not record them.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
